1. Definition 
Customer Relationship Management (CRM) is an integrated business strategy, 
process & technology system for managing interactions with current as well 
as potential customers throughout the customer lifecycle. 
It helps an organization –  
✓ collect customer information 
✓ understand needs 
✓ deliver relevant value 
✓ build profitable long -term 
relationships 
It rests on 2 core functions - 
1. Store what you know about 
each customer 
2. Act on that knowledge to serve the right person, at the right moment, 
through the right channel. 
 
Thus CRM is more than software. Effective CRM combines people, customer-
focused processes, data & technology. 
CRM = PEOPLE + CUSTOMER SATISFACTION + DATA + TECHNOLOGY 
 
2. Objectives of CRM 
• Identify, contact, attract & acquire new customers. 
• Understand customer  (needs, preferences, purchase history  & buying 
behaviour). 
• Improve service quality through timely & personalized support. 
• Increase customer satisfaction, loyalty & retention. 
• Increase revenue through repeat purchase, cross-selling & up-selling. 
• Reduce customer churn by recognizing dissatisfaction or inactivity. 
• Support informed decision-making with customer data & analytics. 
 
3. Evolution of CRM 
Customer Relationship Management (CRM) has evolved significantly since 
its origins in the 1980s. It began as simple contact management  - digital 
rolodexes storing basic customer details. The early 1990s introduced Sales

4. Strategic Role of CRM 
CRM is a software which has strategic capability in organizations to - 
• Centralize customer intelligence:  Maintain a single, unified view of each 
customer with their identity, buying behaviour, transactions, interactions  
etc. to make informed decisions. 
• Helps in the CLC: Systematically move customers through – 
identify → segment → acquire → onboard → serve → retain → grow 
• Personalize at scale:  Use segmentation ( eg., RFM, CLV, personas) & 
analytics to tailor offers, messages & service. 
• Optimize revenue levers:  Shorten sales cycles, improve conversion, 
increase retention & unlock cross-sell/upsell opportunities. 
• Enable data -driven strategy:  Turn interaction data into insights for 
product development, pricing, channel mix  & customer experience 
improvements. 
Example - A retail company uses a cloud -
based CRM system  to analyses & study  
CLV, then high-value customers receive 
early-access offers, while customers who 
have stopped buying receive special offers 
to encourage them to return. 
5. Significance of CRM 
• Better customer knowledge: Organizations understand needs, preferences 
& purchasing behaviour. 
• Higher satisfaction & loyalty: Consistent & personalized interactions 
improve the customer experience. 
• Improved retention: Proactive support & loyalty actions. 
• Greater sales & profitability: Sales teams manage leads better & identify 
cross-sell & up-sell opportunities. 
• Improved efficiency: Automation reduces repetitive work such as follow -
ups, campaign scheduling & ticket routing. 
• Data-driven decisions: CRM reports help evaluate campaign results, sales 
performance, customer value & service quality. 
• Better interdepartmental coordination:  All relevant teams can work 
from shared customer information.

6. Benefits of CRM 
CRM delivers value across all categories of business in the following aspects - 
 
6.1. Customer-Related Benefits 
• 360° customer view:  All customer data like purchases, interactions, 
complaints & p references are  stored in one place, so any employee can 
quickly understand the full history of a customer instead of asking them to 
repeat information. 
• Personalized customer experience:  Offers, recommendations & 
communication can be tailored to individual preferences which makes 
customers feel understood & valued. 
• Improved customer satisfaction & loyalty: Consistent, relevant & timely 
service builds trust over time, making customers less likely to switch to a 
competitor. 
• Faster resolution of queries & complaints:  Organized case tracking 
ensures that no customer request is lost & that complaints are escalated & 
resolved within a defined time frame. 
 
6.2. Sales-Related Benefits 
• Better lead management:  Leads are captured, scored & followed up 
systematically, resulting in higher conversion rates compared to manual 
tracking. 
• Cross-selling & Up-selling opportunities: Purchase history reveals which 
additional products or higher -value versions a customer is likely to be 
interested in. 
• More accurate Sales Forecasting: Pipeline data (deals in progress, their 
stage & probability of closing) allows managers to predict reliable revenue. 
• Shorter sales cycles: Automated reminders & follow -ups ensure that 
prospects are not forgotten, reducing the time it takes to close a deal. 
 
6.3. Marketing-Related Benefits 
• Targeted & Segmented Campaigns: Customers can be grouped by 
behaviour, location, or preferences, so that campaigns reach the audience 
most likely to respond. 
• Measurable Campaign ROI:  CRM systems can track which campaigns 
actually led to sales, helping marketers justify & improve spending.

Course Code: CBS4142                                              Module 1 -  Fundamentals Of Customer Relationship Management 
 Page 6 of 21 
• Improved Segmentation using Analytics: Patterns in customer data 
reveal segments that may not be obvious from intuition alone, improving 
the relevance of every message sent. 
 
6.4. Operational / Organizational Benefits 
• Reduced data silos: Centralized customer data means sales, marketing & 
service teams are no longer working from separate, inconsistent records. 
• Better inter -departmental coordination:  a shared view of the customer 
helps teams hand off work smoothly, eg. when a marketing lead becomes a 
sales opportunity. 
• Task automation: Routine work such as data entry, follow -up emails & 
reminders is automated, saving time & reducing human error. 
• Better resource allocation: Management can direct staff & budget toward 
the customer segments & activities that generate the most value. 
 
6.5. Strategic Benefits 
• Competitive advantage: Deep customer insight is difficult for competitors 
to copy, especially once it is built up over years of interaction data. 
• Increased CLV:  Stronger long -term relationships  with customers 
generates more revenue over their lifetime with the company. 
• Data-driven strategic decisions: Leadership can base decisions on actual 
customer behaviour & trends rather than assumptions. 
• Stronger brand reputation:  Consistently positive experiences  through 
CRM, build a brand that customers are willing to recommend to others.

6.6. Case Studies: Solutions Based on Benefits of CRM 
Case Study 1: 
Amazon is a global e -commerce company operating in a market with 
thousands of competing sellers & platforms, making customer retention 
critical to its business model.  However, Amazon uses CRM -driven data 
analytics to track each customer’s browsing history, search behaviour  & past 
purchases. This data powers personalized product recommendations 
(“customers who bought this also bought that”), tailored emails & a shopping 
experience that adapts to the individual. 
Benefit - This primarily reflects the customer -related benefit of an improved, 
personalized experience  & the strategic benefit of increased CLV, since 
satisfied, engaged customers keep returning to the platform. 
Takeaway - Personalization at scale is only possible because customer data 
from many touchpoints is unified which is a core CRM capability. 
 
Case Study 2 
Starbucks operates in a highly competitive café market where switching to 
another coffee outlet involves very little effort for the customer.  Through the 
Starbucks Rewards Program, integrated with it's mobile app, Starbucks 
collects purchase data to offer personalized rewards, order suggestions  & 
targeted promotions based on each customer’s ordering habits. 
Benefit - This demonstrates the customer -related benefit of enhanced loyalty  
& the marketing -related benefit of targeted, relevant promotions that 
encourage repeat visits. 
Takeaway - A loyalty program backed by CRM data turns occasional buyers 
into habitual, engaged customers. 
 
Case Study 3 
The Taj Group operates numerous hotel properties across India & 
internationally & guests often expect the same standard of personalized 
service at every property they visit.  Taj Hotels maintains detailed guest 
profiles like room preferences, dietary needs  & past stay history - that are 
accessible across its properties, allowing staff at any location to recognize & 
cater to a returning guest.

Benefit - This shows the customer-related benefit of a consistent, personalized 
experience across multiple locations, which is a distinctive challenge in the 
hospitality industry. 
Takeaway - Collaborative access to a single guest profile across branches is 
what enables this consistency. 
 
Case Study 4 
Retail banks offer many products like savings accounts, loans, insurance, 
investments & customers rarely use all of them from a single provider unless 
the bank proactively identifies relevant needs.  For eg. ICICI Bank uses CRM 
analytics to study customer transaction patterns & life-stage indicators (such 
as a salary increase or a large withdrawal), allowing relationship managers to 
recommend relevant financial products at the right time. 
Benefit - This illustrates the sales -related benefit of cross -selling & the 
strategic benefit of increased customer profitability, since each retained 
customer generates revenue from multiple products. 
Takeaway - Analytical CRM capability by spotting patterns in transaction 
data is what makes timely cross-selling possible. 
 
Case Study 5 
Food-delivery platforms operate on thin margins & depend heavily on repeat 
orders, making efficient marketing spend with smooth operations essential.  
Swiggy, for eg. uses customer ordering data to personalize restaurant 
recommendations, design targeted promotional offers for specific customer 
segments & plan delivery operations efficiently based on demand patterns. 
Benefit - This demonstrates both the marketing -related benefit of targeted 
campaigns & the operational benefit of centralized, actionable customer data 
feeding into business decisions. 
Takeaway - The same underlying customer data can simultaneously improve 
marketing relevance & day-to-day operational planning.

• CRM stores customers’ Data

• It helps to personalized recommendations, rewards, services, cross -selling 
offers & optimized delivery routes directly to customers 
 
Common Challenges in Realizing These Benefits 
CRM benefits are not automatic  so organizations commonly face challenges 
like – 
• Poor data quality like incomplete or duplicate customer records 
• Low adoption by employees who find the system inconvenient 
• High implementation & training costs 
• Difficulty integrating the CRM with existing systems 
A CRM system only delivers the benefits described above when these 
implementation challenges are managed well. 
 
7. Components of CRM 
A complete CRM system is made up 
of several interconnected 
components which allow an 
organization to capture customer 
centric data relevant to the company, 
act on it & continuously improve the 
customer relationship. 
• Customer Data Management:  
The foundation of any CRM 
system is a  central database 
storing contact details, purchase 
history, preferences  & every 
recorded interaction. Without accurate, well -maintained data, every other 
component becomes less effective. 
• Sales Force Automation (SFA): Tools that help sales teams manage leads, 
track opportunities through each stage of the pipeline, schedule follow -ups 
& generate sales forecasts, reducing dependence on manual spreadsheets. 
• Marketing Automation:  Tools for planning & running campaigns, 
segmenting customers into meaningful groups  & automating email, SMS, 
or app-notification marketing based on customer behaviour.

• Customer Service & Support:  Helpdesk and ticketing systems that log 
customer queries & complaints, assign them to the right team member  & 
track them until resolution, often with defined service-level timelines. 
• Analytics & Reporting:  Dashboards & predictive-analytics tools that 
convert raw customer data into actionable insights, like identifying which 
customers are likely to churn or which products to recommend next. 
• Collaboration Tools: Shared calendars, notes  & communication features 
that keep sales, marketing  & service teams aligned on the current status of 
each customer, avoiding duplicated or contradictory outreach. 
• Technology Infrastructure:  The underlying cloud platform, mobile 
access, security controls  & integration capability that connect the CRM 
with other business systems such as ERP (Enterprise Resource Planning) or 
billing software. 
 
8. Types of CRM 
• Operational CRM  - Operational CRM automates & streamlines day -to-
day, customer-facing business processes in sales, marketing  & service. It is 
the “front office” side of CRM, focused mainly on execution. 
Example: 
a. Salesforce Sales Cloud used for lead & opportunity tracking 
b. Zoho CRM used by Indian SMEs for daily sales & follow-up management 
c. Ticketing system of the cal l-centre of a bank that logs & routes customer 
service requests 
 
• Analytical CRM - Analytical CRM focuses on collecting and  analyzing 
customer data (from operational CRM and other sources) to generate 
insights that support decision -making – such as customer segmentation, 
churn prediction, and campaign targeting. 
Example: 
a. Amazon’s recommendation engine analyses browsing & purchase data to 
predict what a customer is likely to buy next 
b. A bank  analyzing transaction history to build credit -risk or cross -sell 
scores 
c. Use of dashboards to identify which customer segments are most likely to 
churn or not return

• Collaborative CRM  - Collaborative CRM focuses on sharing customer 
information across departments, channels, and even external partners, so 
that everyone interacting with the customer has consistent, up -to-date 
information. 
Examples: 
a. A Telecom company share customer complaint history to all call-centre 
b. Retail stores & social media support team 
c. An airline sharing passenger data across its booking system, check -in 
counters & in-flight service team

8.1. Relationship Between the 3 types if CRM 
 
9. Strategic Importance of CRM in Business 
CRM is a customer centric business strategy software tool  of organizational 
decision-making. It’s strategic importance stems from several factors – 
• It is significantly cheaper to retain an existing customer than to acquire a 
new one, so a strong CRM strategy directly protects revenue 
• Customer data is   treated as a strategic asset that informs product design, 
pricing & service decisions at the highest levels of the organization 
• In markets where competing products are mostly similar, the customer  
relationship quality becomes the most important  parameter for 
differentiation

Course Code: CBS4142                                              Module 1 -  Fundamentals Of Customer Relationship Management 
 Page 13 of 21 
• CRM supports broader long-term goals like brand loyalty, customer-centric 
innovation & alignment with digital transformation initiatives across the 
organization. 
 
9.1. Global Examples 
Amazon (USA): Amazon treats customer data as a core strategic asset, using 
it to drive personalized recommendations, pricing & marketing. This 
customer-centric strategy is widely regarded as central to its ability to 
compete across many product categories simultaneously. 
 
Apple (USA):  Apple builds long -term customer relationships through an 
integrated ecosystem of devices & services, supported by AppleCare & in-
store Genius Bar assistance. This relationship -driven strategy encourages 
repeat purchases & strong brand loyalty rather than one-off transactions. 
 
Marriott International (USA):  Marriott uses its Marriott Bonvoy loyalty 
program, backed by CRM systems, to retain guests across it ’s large global 
portfolio of hotel brands, personalizing offers based on each guest’s stay 
history & preferences. 
 
Coca-Cola (USA/Global):  Coca-Cola uses CRM & loyalty initiatives to 
engage consumers directly, gather feedback & tailor marketing campaigns to 
different regional markets, supporting it ’s strategy of maintaining relevance 
across highly diverse customer bases. 
 
9.2. Indian Examples 
Tata Motors:  Tata Motors uses CRM systems to coordinate after -sales 
service & maintenance reminders across it ’s dealer network, strengthening 
long-term customer relationships in a sector where trust in service quality 
strongly influences repeat purchase. 
 
ICICI Bank:  ICICI Bank uses CRM analytics to understand customer life -
stage needs & cross -sell appropriate banking, insurance & investment 
products, making customer retention & share -of-wallet a strategic priority in 
retail banking. 
 
Reliance Jio: Reliance Jio uses CRM and customer data analytics to manage 
large-scale customer acquisition & retention strategies, which has been

Course Code: CBS4142                                              Module 1 -  Fundamentals Of Customer Relationship Management 
 Page 14 of 21 
strategically important in a highly price -sensitive & competitive Indian 
telecom market. 
 
Flipkart: Flipkart uses CRM -driven personalization to recommend products, 
manage customer support & design targeted offers for millions of e-commerce 
customers, treating customer experience as a key differentiator against 
domestic & global competitors. 
 
Taj Group (Indian Hotels Company Ltd.):  The Taj Group uses its Taj 
InnerCircle loyalty program, supported by CRM systems, to differentiate itself 
strategically in the Indian hospitality sector through consistently personalized 
guest experiences across properties. 
 
9.3. Why This Matters Strategically? 
Two points are worth emphasizing for a business systems student. 
• CRM is tied directly to a specific strategic goal or objectives – 
Differentiation (Apple) 
Retention in a price-sensitive market (Reliance Jio) 
Cross-selling to increase share-of-wallet (ICICI Bank) 
Consistent brand experience across locations (Marriott, Taj Group) 
• The scale at which these companies operate , millions of customers across 
multiple channels, makes a technology-supported CRM strategy a necessity 
rather than a choice & it is to be noted that relationship management at this 
scale would not be possible through manual effort alone. 
 
10. CRM vs Traditional Marketing 
Customer Relationship Management (CRM) & Traditional Marketing differ 
fundamentally in orientation, data use & measurement. While CRM is 
customer-centric, data-driven & relationship-focused, Traditional Marketing is 
product-centric, broadcast-oriented & campaign-focused. 
• CRM treats the customer as the central unit of strategy. It integrates sales, 
marketing & service data into a single system of record &  , a system of 
intelligence. It uses behavio ural & transactional data to trigger relevant 
communications like welcome series, cart -abandonment reminders, 
replenishment alerts, loyalty rewards, across the customer lifecycle.

Course Code: CBS4142                                              Module 1 -  Fundamentals Of Customer Relationship Management 
 Page 15 of 21 
• Traditional Marketing emerged in an era of mass media, where firms 
competed primarily on product features, price & brand visibility. It’s logic 
is linear – create a compelling message, buy media space with the hope that 
the right people (target audience) will see it at the right time.  Traditional 
Marketing ex cels at building awareness & shaping brand perceptions at 
scale, especially for new products or markets  but it s truggles with 
precision, real-time optimization & post-campaign relationship building. 
• Strategically, the 2 approaches are complementary.  Traditional marketing 
is powerful for top -of-funnel awareness & brand building, while CRM 
excels at mid  & bottom-funnel conversion, retention  & advocacy. Modern 
organizations blend both: using mass channels to acquire attention & CRM 
systems to convert, nurture & retain those customers over time.

10.1. Integrating CRM & TRADITIONAL MARKETING  Approaches 
In practice, the most effective strategies combine a bit of  both traditional 
marketing & CRM marketing for an unified growth system:  
• Traditional channels are used to create at scale awareness & shape brand 
perception by capturing interest via digital forms, branch sign -ups, call-centre 
interactions while feeding customer data into the CRM  software. 
• CRM is then used to nurture leads, personalize offers  & manage the post -
acquisition journey, continuously optimizing based on behavioural data.

 Page 19 of 21 
This integrated model aligns with the broader shift in marketing from 
'advertising to audiences' toward 'managing relationships with individuals,' 
where CRM   functions as the operational backbone of modern marketing. 
11. Key Drivers of CRM 
Customer relationship management (CRM) is driven by the need to 
understand cu stomers, improve their experience, increase retention  & 
coordinate sales, marketing & service activities. The major drivers are: 
• Increasing customer expectations  - Customers expect fast responses, 
personalized communication, consistent service  & seamless interactions 
across channels. CRM systems help organizations record and use customer 
information to meet these expectations. 
• Demand for personalized marketing  - Businesses use CRM data to 
segment customers, identify preferences, tailor offers, and deliver targeted 
campaigns. Personalization is a major factor behind CRM adoption. 
• Improved customer retention & loyalty - CRM helps organizations 
monitor customer satisfaction, identify potential churn, manage complaints, 
& develop loyalty programmes. Retaining existing customers is often more 
cost-effective than acquiring new ones. 
• Centralization of customer data  - CRM integrates information from 
sales, marketing, customer service, websites, social media  & other 
touchpoints into a unified customer record. This supports a more complete 
or “360-degree” view of the customer. 
• Sales-force automation  - CRM automates lead tracking, follow -up 
reminders, opportunity management, pipeline monitoring  & sales 
forecasting. This reduces administrative work & improves sales 
productivity. 
• Growth of digital & omnichannel commerce  - The expansion of e -
commerce, mobile applications, social media, email  & online customer 
service has increased the number of customer interaction points. CRM 
allows organizations to coordinate these interactions across channels. 
• Use of artificial intelligence & analytics - AI-enabled CRM systems can 
generate customer insights, predict purchasing behaviour, recommend next 
actions, automate responses  & identify potential churn. The integration of

 Page 20 of 21 
AI & demand for real -time insights are important contemporary growth 
drivers. 
• Cloud computing & remote work  - Cloud-based CRM offers scalable 
access, lower infrastructure requirements, easier updates  & support for 
geographically distributed teams. These advantages have accelerated 
adoption among both large organizations & small to medium-sized 
enterprises. 
• Need for operational efficiency & automation - Organizations adopt 
CRM to automate repetitive marketing, sales  & service processes, reduce 
errors, improve communication & lower operating costs. 
• Need for data -driven decision -making - CRM analytics provide 
information about customer behaviour, campaign performance, sales 
conversion, service quality & revenue trends. Managers can therefore make 
decisions based on evidence rather than intuition. 
• Integration with other business systems  - CRM platforms integrate with 
enterprise resource planning, marketing automation, customer -data 
platforms, communication tools, payment systems  & business intelligence 
software to improve information flow across the organization. 
 
11.1. Internal drivers of successful CRM implementation 
Successful CRM depends on technology & the followings: 
o Senior-management support. 
o Employee training & participation. 
o User-friendly workflows. 
o High-quality & accurate customer data. 
o Integration with existing systems. 
o Clear performance objectives. 
o Incentives that encourage consistent usage. 
o Strong privacy, security & data-governance practices. 
 
Note: CRM adoption commonly fails when the system does not fit 
employees’ workflows, creates excessive manual data entry or does not 
provide clear benefits to users.

7. Enablers of Customer Relationship Management (CRM) 
Enabler Main contribution 
People Skills, participation, training & adoption 
Processes Standardized & customer-focused workflows 
Technology Integration, automation, accessibility & scalability 
Data Reliable information for coordination & decisions 
Strategy Alignment between CRM activities & business goals 
Culture Collaboration, customer orientation & willingness to change 
Governance Privacy, security, accountability & performance control 
 
Therefore, CRM is enabled not by software alone but by the alignment of 
people, processes, technology, data & organizational strategy. A sophisticated 
CRM platform will produce limited benefits if employees do not adopt it, 
departments do not share information or the underlying customer data is 
unreliable. 
Key Terms for SAQ 
CRM: A strategy, process & technology approach for managing customer interactions & building long-
term relationships. 
Customer lifecycle: The stages through which a customer progresses: identify, segment, acquire, 
onboard, serve, retain & grow. 
Touchpoint: Any interaction point between a customer & organization, such as a website, store, call 
centre, email or social media. 
Segmentation: Dividing customers into groups with similar needs, characteristics or behaviours. 
CLV: Customer Lifetime Value  - total  revenue or profit from a customer over the entire relationship  
with the company. 
Sales Force Automation (SFA): Automation of sales activities such as lead management, opportunity 
tracking & forecasting. 
Marketing automation: Use of technology to plan, deliver & measure campaigns & nurture leads. 
Service automation: Tools for cases, tickets, knowledge bases, chat support  & customer issue 
resolution. 
360-degree customer view: A unified customer profile containing identity,  transactions, preferences & 
interaction history across channels. 
Cross-selling: Offering related or complementary products to an existing customer. 
Up-selling: Encouraging a customer to buy a upgraded version. 
Churn: Loss of customers. 
AI-enabled CRM: CRM that uses AI for prediction, personalization, recommendations, chatbots  & 
automation.
